text: A neural network is a stack of functions, each feeding its output into the next. To train it, we need the slope of the whole stack, and the chain rule tells us how to build it from the slopes of the pieces. The short version is that rates multiply.

Think of three gears meshed together. If the middle gear turns twice for each turn of the first, and the last gear turns three times for each turn of the middle, then the last gear turns six times for each turn of the first. No calculus is needed to see this; the rates simply multiply as the motion passes along.

Now with functions. Let u equal three x, and let y equal u squared, so that y is a function of a function of x. A small nudge to x is magnified three times by the time it reaches u, and that change in u is then magnified by two u on its way to y. Multiply the two rates and you have the derivative of the whole chain: d y by d x equals d y by d u, times d u by d x.

The notation makes this look like cancelling fractions, which is a fine memory aid, but the real content is the picture of a nudge travelling down the chain and being scaled at every link. Each link uses its own slope at the point where the signal currently sits, which is why the inner function has to be evaluated first.

Take a longer chain, the kind found in a single artificial neuron. Multiply the input by a weight, add a bias, and squash the result with a smooth function such as the sigmoid. Changing the weight changes the sum, the sum changes the squashed output, and the output changes the error, so the slope of the error with respect to the weight is the product of the local slopes along the way.

This suggests an efficient order of work. Run the chain forwards once, storing every intermediate value, then walk backwards from the error, multiplying local slopes as you go, so that each link is visited only once. That backward walk is called backpropagation, and it is nothing more than the chain rule applied in a sensible order.

A large language model is a chain with hundreds of links, and training it means running exactly this backward walk through every layer, for every batch of text it reads. Next, we let a function take several inputs at once, and meet partial derivatives.
